sources.title: From French outpost to Euro-Canadian corridor? Why Carney and Macron met in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon

discussion.body: The Conversation Canada frames the setting as the substance: the visit brought together a contentious shared history, Canada's rapprochement with Europe and the archipelago's search for new development opportunities, with France and Canada seeking closer ties amid growing tensions with the United States.
Part of that backdrop: Trump has repeatedly threatened to make Canada a 51st state and recently posted a map depicting an expanded U.S. encompassing Canada, Greenland and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon.

An archipelago of 242 square kilometres and around 6,000 people is not a market or a base in any ordinary accounting. Being drawn onto someone else's map is a strange route to strategic relevance, but it is a route.

items.title: Carney Met Macron on French Soil, 25 Kilometres Off Newfoundland
items.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney did not need to cross the Atlantic to meet Emmanuel Macron on French soil over the weekend. He joined the French president in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, just 25 kilometres off Newfoundland — the first official visit to the archipelago by a Canadian prime minister. A first visit is easy to dismiss as ceremonial trivia; it is also a measure of how long a relationship went without one.

sources.title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry

items.title: The Bayeux Tapestry's New Rule: No Photographs, Please
items.body: The British Museum has banned visitors from photographing the Bayeux Tapestry, the BBC reports, and the objection is to the standing still rather than the camera: visitors stopping to take pictures of the 68-metre medieval embroidery were holding up others, prompting the rule change. Sixty-eight metres is a long time to spend behind someone composing a shot.

sources.title: Johnson Space Center Sparks Curiosity at Houston’s 33rd Annual Japan Festival

items.title: Artemis III's Crew, on Display at a Houston Festival
items.body: On Sept. 12-13, NASA's Johnson Space Center employees brought space exploration to Houston's Japan Festival at Hermann Park. Their booth showcased the upcoming Artemis III mission and its crew, along with NASA's plans for the Moon Base. It is the unglamorous half of spaceflight — a display, a booth and a conversation — and the half that decides whether anyone outside the agency is paying attention.

sources.title: This farm raised thousands of pigs for slaughter. Now it's growing mushrooms instead

items.title: An Iowa Farm Trades Pigs for Mushrooms
items.body: The U.S. gets nearly a third of its pork from Iowa. NPR reports that one family there is making the switch from pigs to specialty mushrooms, which the network describes as more sustainable, and is trying to show other pig farmers how it did it. Teaching the neighbours may be the harder half of the project: a new crop is one thing, a new crop with company is another.

sources.title: 'Just plain panic': Fears mount as N.B. considers restricting U.S. hunters, anglers

discussion.body: Using recreational licences as trade-war leverage is a strange choice precisely because the spending at stake — guiding fees, tags, lodge nights — happens on the Canadian side of the line.
The surprise is the more revealing detail than the restriction. Whatever the merits of the policy, a measure aimed at Washington lands on people in the province who had no warning it was coming.

items.title: New Brunswick Weighs Licence Curbs on U.S. Hunters and Anglers
items.body: New Brunswick has moved to possibly restrict hunting and fishing licences as part of its response to the ongoing trade war with the United States, and the people on both sides of that border say they were caught off guard by it, CBC reports. American hunters and anglers and New Brunswick outfitters were among those surprised by the proposal. The trade war is the stated reason, which makes a fish-and-game office an unlikely instrument of foreign policy — but a licence is one of the few levers a province can pull without touching tariffs or procurement. The awkward part is who pays first: outfitting businesses, lodges and guides on the Canadian side earn their living from the same visitors a restriction would keep out, which may be why the surprise registered so loudly among New Brunswick operators rather than only among Americans.

sources.title: Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'

discussion.body: The interesting thing isn't who is right about extinction risk; it's that the industry's most prominent voice on the subject is also its most exposed. That doesn't settle the question, but it shapes how the answer travels.
Exposure cuts both ways. The same person is best placed to see what the systems can actually do, which is exactly the vantage point researchers warning about long-run risk don't have.

items.title: Nvidia's Huang Calls AI Extinction Warnings a Doomsday Narrative
items.body: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has rejected fears that artificial intelligence could lead to human extinction, characterizing them as doomsday narratives, the BBC reports. His comments follow warnings from AI researchers that the technology could lead to human extinction. That contrast is worth keeping in view: one side's warning and the other side's reassurance are both forecasts about a technology still being built, and the person doing the reassuring runs the company whose business depends on AI being built. Stake is not the same as error — a chipmaker could be right about the odds — but it does mean the reassurances should be weighed as a position, not as a neutral assessment.

sources.title: Tobias Forge’s ‘V/H/S Mixtape’ Segment, Swedish Horror ‘Trespassers,’ ‘The End’ by ‘Midsommar’ Production Designer on Mylla Films Slate (EXCLUSIVE)

items.title: A Swedish Genre Label's Pitch: the Talent Comes to Us
items.body: Mylla Films, a Swedish boutique genre outfit, was launched at Cannes in 2022 by Patrik Andersson — a producer on Midsommar — and Jakob Abrahamsson, chief executive of the Nordic distributor NonStop Entertainment. Since then, Variety reports, it has become a draw for Nordic genre talent: Abrahamsson says people with substantial CVs and filmographies have been reaching out to the label rather than waiting to be courted. For a small company, that is the whole business model in one sentence. A boutique label cannot outbid anyone for projects; what it can offer is a short path to people who already know how to make this kind of film.

discussion.body: The useful part is that it applies to action, not just belief. You can move decisively on a strong probability without pretending the probability is a guarantee.
That advice is easier to follow when the cost of being wrong is a changed mind. When the cost is a bridge that falls down, 'never certain' starts to sound like a luxury of the seminar room.

items.title: Cicero's Case for Being Confident Without Being Certain
items.body: In an essay for Aeon, Massimo Pigliucci argues that Cicero's life and thought are a testament to probabilia: the position that we should be confident in our beliefs, but never certain of them. The distinction does real work, because confidence and certainty get treated as the same currency in most arguments. Confidence is a strength of commitment — enough to act, decide, and defend a position. Certainty is a claim about the possibility of being wrong, and it is the part probabilia asks you to give up. What remains is a stance that permits decisive action while leaving the door open to revision, which is harder to perform than either dogmatism or shrugging.

sources.title: Pablo Larraín Ventures Into Argentina With His San Sebastián Golden Shell Contender ‘My Sad Dead’

discussion.body: The geography is the headline here: a Chilean director working in Argentina for the first time, on stories by an Argentine writer.
The cast backs that up — Mercedes Morán, Dolores Fonzi, Alejandra Flechner and Carolina Álvarez, an Argentine ensemble rather than imported names.

items.title: Pablo Larraín's First Argentina Film Adapts Three Mariana Enriquez Stories
items.body: Pablo Larraín, the writer-director best known for the trilogy Jackie, Spencer and Maria, ventures into Argentina for the first time with My Sad Dead (Mis muertos tristes), adapted from three stories by the Argentine writer Mariana Enriquez. The cast is led by Mercedes Morán, Dolores Fonzi, Alejandra Flechner and Carolina Álvarez, described as some of Argentina's brightest talent. Larraín's reputation rests on portraits of celebrated women; this project trades that for an Argentine writer's short fiction and an Argentine ensemble, so the change in source material is at least as interesting as the change in border. Three stories is also a structural question: whether they braid into one film or sit alongside each other is the thing to watch.

sources.title: Rental rules in Ontario change today. Here’s what tenants and landlords need to know

items.title: Ontario Shortens the Clock for Tenants Landlords Say Owe Rent
items.body: A batch of changes to Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act comes into force Monday, including shorter deadlines for tenants whom landlords say have fallen behind on rent payments. Deadlines inside a dispute are not neutral housekeeping: shortening a tenant's window to answer an arrears claim hands the practical advantage to whoever files first, and a landlord is the one who files. It is one item in a wider package, and the one with the most immediate effect on a tenancy already in conflict.

sources.title: What to know as world leaders converge at the United Nations this week

items.title: Guterres Returns for a Final General Assembly as Diplomacy Falters
items.body: António Guterres returns to New York for his final U.N. General Assembly, with diplomacy faltering over wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and the global body facing deep divisions, NPR reports. A last assembly for a sitting secretary-general is a natural occasion for stocktaking, and this one arrives with two live wars on the agenda. The divisions described here belong to the membership rather than to the departing secretary-general, which is why the farewell is a milestone for the office more than a turning point for the institution.

sources.title: Pickering nuclear reactors start coming off-line for massive refurbishment

items.title: An Ontario Nuclear Plant Starts a Refurbishment as the Province Bets on Reactors
items.body: Global News Canada reports that an Ontario nuclear plant is beginning a massive refurbishment project, with Doug Ford's government looking to lean heavily on nuclear energy to serve the province's electricity needs. It is the slow, expensive kind of nuclear commitment: work on a plant that already exists rather than a promise of something new on the grid.

sources.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico say they've notified Trump they're suing over denied White House access

items.title: Three News Outlets Tell Trump They're Suing Over Denied White House Access
items.body: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say they have notified President Donald Trump that they are suing over denied White House access, according to PBS NewsHour. The outlet characterizes the move as a clear escalation of Trump's long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and as the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition

items.title: Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Film Festival Cancels Its 2026 Edition
items.body: The Red Sea Film Foundation has cancelled the 2026 edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival, saying in a statement that the sixth edition had been postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027, Deadline reports. The edition had been scheduled for December 3–12, and the announcement followed weeks of speculation about whether it would go ahead. A postponement to late 2027 keeps the festival on the calendar rather than ending it; what changes for the filmmakers and sales agents who had planned around a December slot is another matter.

sources.title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Revisits The Character That Won Him An Oscar In David Fincher’s Latest

items.title: A Fincher-Directed Cliff Booth Film Gets a Trailer and an IMAX Window
items.body: The first trailer is out for David Fincher's The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino. The release plan Deadline reports is a two-stage one: a premiere in IMAX on November 25 for a two-week engagement, followed by release on the streamer on December 23. A fortnight of big-format exclusivity before streaming is the interesting part — it treats the theatrical window as an event rather than a formality.

sources.title: ‘Stitched it back’: Edmonton event where locals mend clothes promotes sustainability

items.title: Mending Thrift-Store Pants as a Small Stand Against Fast Fashion
items.body: Pearce Carpenter says fixing the holes in the black balloon bottoms they bought from an Edmonton thrift store is their way of tackling fast fashion. Repair is the least glamorous kind of environmentalism: no new technology, no policy lever, just thread and an hour, and one garment that keeps going instead of being replaced. What makes the gesture interesting is the choice inside it. Mending is rarely forced — it happens because someone decided the thing was worth keeping. A thrift-store find repaired by hand is a small argument about value, made in a world where replacement is often cheaper than repair.

discussion.body: An archive of sound is a document, not a substitute. You can replay an hour of forest, but you can't replay the process that produced it.
A document is still worth having. If the sounds go, a recording is the only thing left that lets anyone hear what was there.

items.title: The Race to Record a Rainforest Before Its Sounds Are Gone
items.body: Indonesia is building a new capital city, and according to Aeon, the race is on to preserve the sounds of the rainforest before they vanish forever. Sound is an awkward thing to put in a conservation plan, because it can't be banked like a seed. A recording doesn't hold the forest; it holds one microphone's account of a stretch of time — this chorus, at this hour — and that becomes valuable precisely because the place itself is changing. There's a deadline built into the project: the capital is coming, and a recording made later would capture a different forest. Archiving is usually what you do when you have time. Here the construction schedule sets the clock.

discussion.body: The heaviest thing in metal might turn out to be a seated elder and a weeping fan. Durability, not menace.
Or sentiment is just easy at the end of anything. The real test of 'metal' is whether it survives a random Tuesday.

items.title: Crying at a Seated Ozzy: The Softness of Metal
items.body: Keith Kahn-Harris, writing on Psyche, describes watching a seated Ozzy Osbourne play his final gig while he himself had a broken ankle, in tears, and concludes it couldn't have been more metal. His essay is titled 'The softness of metal', and the scene makes the case for that title. The genre's pose is invulnerability; its most fitting moment here is a performer who can't stand and a fan who can't either, both openly undone. Devotion looks like this at the end of a long career — less a wall of noise than a gathering of people who came to feel something together. Nothing about tears at the last gig contradicts the hardness. It may be what the hardness was for.
